Used by the cross-source threads tests and eval.

segments.text: Today a skeptic on the AI margin story joins us to push back on last week's guest.
I disagree with the claim that falling inference costs expand gross margins.
Unit economics do not improve when every competitor gets the same cost curve at the same time.
Pricing power is not the mechanism here; buyers capture the savings within two quarters.
So my falsifiable claim is the opposite: margins will not expand, they will compress back to forty percent.
Watch the gross margins next quarter and you will see the competition show up.
Capital allocation follows: the winners will reinvest the savings, not bank them.
That is a base rate every software cycle has followed.
The cost curve falls for everyone, so it is not a moat.
Quick detour: the green room had a new espresso machine and nobody could work it.
We spent ten minutes on whose turn it was to pick lunch and which playlist to put on.
Somebody brought a dog, which became the highlight of the afternoon for everyone.
Then a long debate about the best airport lounge, which settled nothing.
Anyway, back to it.
On market structure I think last week's guest is wrong about the licenses.
The licenses are not a durable moat; regulators will issue more of them within a year.
Pricing power that depends on a regulatory catalyst is borrowed, not owned.
When the next two players get licenses, margins revert and the price takers catch up.
Labor is the real cost curve to watch, and AI compresses it for every competitor equally.
My capital allocation advice: do not pay a premium for a moat a regulator can revoke.
That claim is falsifiable within four quarters, and I expect to be proven right.
